proposed_subjects.title: Dispersion relations for an absolutely continuous integrable causal kernel
proposed_subjects.statement: Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$ and let $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be a locally absolutely continuous matrix kernel with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (entrywise integrability), and let $$\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds\qquad(\operatorname{Im}z>0)$$ be the matrix response function. Here locally absolutely continuous means that each real entry restricted to every compact interval $[a,b]\subseteq[0,\infty)$ satisfies the finite disjoint-interval condition of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]: for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $\sum_\ell(v_\ell-u_\ell)<\delta$ implies $\sum_\ell|K_{jk}(v_\ell)-K_{jk}(u_\ell)|<\epsilon$ for every finite family with disjoint interiors. $K\prime$ denotes the almost-everywhere derivative, with any measurable zero extension on its null exceptional set. Then the entries of $\chi$ are holomorphic functions on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-domain]]), continuous and $C^1$ on its real boundary, bounded on the closed upper half-plane with $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K'_{jk}\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$, and the entrywise principal-value dispersion formulas hold: for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi .$$ The sharper bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le(|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K\prime_{jk}\|_1)/|z|$ holds for every nonzero $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$. Here $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$ means $\lim_{R\to\infty}\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}(\int_{\omega-R}^{\omega-\eta}+\int_{\omega+\eta}^{\omega+R})F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$; the tails converge absolutely, so the choice of centering at infinity does not change the limit. For an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ define the total transfer function $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}:=\chi_\infty+\chi$; the formulas then apply to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$; the scalar case is $d=1$. Causality alone supplies neither growth assumptions beyond those stated nor the passivity quadratic-form condition, which is a separate model assertion.
proposed_subjects.strategy:
Treat each real entry $k=K_{jk}$ separately. Its locally absolutely continuous representative is the one in the statement; the published [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] applies on $[0,N]$ under the declared Countable Choice and Dependent Choice and yields $k(s)=k(0)+\int_0^s k\prime(u)du$. Since $k\prime\in L^1$, dominated convergence shows this has a finite limit $\ell=k(0)+\int_0^\infty k\prime$. If $\ell\ne0$, then $|k(s)|\ge|\ell|/2$ for all sufficiently large $s$, contradicting $k\in L^1$ by monotonicity of the integral ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Hence $k(s)\to0$.
The defining integral is bounded by $\|k\|_1$ on $\overline H$, and dominated convergence gives joint continuity there ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Writing $z=x+iy$, the real parameter derivatives of $k(s)e^{izs}$ are $isk(s)e^{izs}$ and $-sk(s)e^{izs}$. On any rectangle in $H$ their absolute values are bounded by $s|k(s)|$, integrable by hypothesis. [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied separately in $x,y$ supplies the partials; dominated convergence makes them continuous, and $\partial_y\chi=i\partial_x\chi$ gives holomorphy by [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]]. Along the real boundary the same theorem in the real parameter and the same majorant give the continuous derivative $\chi\prime(\omega)=\int_0^\infty isk(s)e^{i\omega s}ds$.
For fixed $z\ne0$, the real and imaginary parts of $g(s):=e^{izs}$ are $C^1$ on each $[0,N]$, hence absolutely continuous by [[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]]. Apply [[thm-integration-by-parts-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] separately to $(k,\operatorname{Re}g)$ and $(k,\operatorname{Im}g)$ and combine the real identities to get
$$\int_0^N k(s)e^{izs}ds=\frac{k(N)e^{izN}-k(0)}{iz}-\frac1{iz}\int_0^N k\prime(s)e^{izs}ds.$$
This is Lebesgue integration by parts for AC functions, not the ordinary everywhere-differentiable Riemann theorem. For $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, $|e^{izs}|\le1$; $k(N)\to0$ kills the endpoint term and dominated convergence applies to both integrals. Thus
$$\chi_{jk}(z)=-\frac{k(0)}{iz}-\frac1{iz}\int_0^\infty k\prime(s)e^{izs}ds,\qquad |\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\frac{|k(0)|+\|k\prime\|_1}{|z|}.$$
For completeness the boundary contour step is valid for any scalar $F$ holomorphic on $H:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on $\overline H$, with $C^1$ real boundary restriction and $F(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on $\overline H$ at infinity. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$. Use the real intervals from $\omega-R$ to $\omega-\eta$ and $\omega+\eta$ to $\omega+R$, a clockwise upper semicircle of radius $\eta$ about $\omega$, and the counterclockwise large upper semicircle of radius $R$ about $\omega$. For $\delta>0$ apply [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]] to $F(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ on $D_\delta:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$. This open domain is star-shaped about any point $\omega+iA$, $A>0$, so the contour is null-homotopic there and the integrand is holomorphic. All contour pieces lie in $D_\delta$; no analytic extension of $F$ across the real boundary is assumed. On each fixed contour, continuity on a compact closed-half-plane neighborhood gives $F(z+i\delta)\to F(z)$ uniformly as $\delta\downarrow0$ by [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], and [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]] transfers the zero contour identity to $F(z)/(z-\omega)$. The large arc has $|z-\omega|=R$, $|z|\ge R-|\omega|$ and length $\pi R$, hence its contribution is $O(1/R)$. Parametrizing the clockwise small arc by $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$ gives $-i\pi F(\omega)+o(1)$. Locally the divided difference $[F(\xi)-F(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded because the boundary is $C^1$; the constant term cancels under the symmetric indentation. The tails are absolutely integrable by $F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)=O(|\xi|^{-2})$. First $\eta\downarrow0$, then $R\to\infty$ therefore gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi F(\omega)$ and the two real/imaginary formulas. Apply the preceding step to each entry of $\chi$. Adding the stipulated real instantaneous matrix means the total transfer function is $\chi_\infty+\chi$; subtract $\chi_\infty$ before taking the principal values. All scalar claims are the $d=1$ case. Neither temporal causality nor these analytic identities impose the separate passivity quadratic-form condition.

proposed_subjects.title: Dispersion relations for a finitely subtracted analytic response
proposed_subjects.statement: Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $\omega_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\chi$ be holomorphic on the upper half-plane and continuous on its closure, of class $C^1$ on its real boundary away from $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfying $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ outside a compact set ([[def-complex-domain]]). Let $P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)(z-\omega_0)^j/j!$ be the Taylor polynomial at $\omega_0$ and $f(z)=[\chi(z)-P(z)]/(z-\omega_0)^n$, with the removable value at $\omega_0$. Assume the boundary restriction of $f$ is class $C^1$ (the local holomorphy supplies this at $\omega_0$). Then for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Re}P(\omega)+\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,$$ $$\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}P(\omega)-\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi.$$ At $\omega=\omega_0$ the formula is read as the stated Taylor value. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is also valid with $P=0$, $f=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and the factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ for all $\omega$; at $\omega_0$ use the same principal-value formula rather than a Taylor-value convention. For the separate constitutive polynomial branch assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]), let $A_0,\ldots,A_m$ be real scalar coefficients or real matrices, and let $K$ satisfy all hypotheses of [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]. On histories with bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$, the response $\sum_{j=0}^m A_jE^{(j)}+K*E$ is causal, and its transfer function in the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z):=\sum_{j=0}^m A_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared polynomial $Q$ leaves the proved entrywise dispersion formulas for $\chi_K$; this branch does not require holomorphic continuation through a real subtraction point. The Taylor-subtracted formulas above apply to the total response when its additional local-holomorphy, growth and boundary hypotheses are satisfied; $Q$ need not equal its Taylor polynomial $P$. General passivity and storage remain separate model conditions.
proposed_subjects.strategy:
[[thm-taylor-expansion-holomorphic-function]] on a complex neighborhood of $\omega_0$ shows that $\chi-P$ has a zero of order at least $n$, so division gives the holomorphic removable continuation of $f$ there. Elsewhere in $H$ its denominator is nonzero. Continuity of $\chi$ on $\overline H$ and the removable continuation make $f$ continuous on $\overline H$; its real restriction is $C^1$ by hypothesis. The growth bound on $\chi$ and the degree of $P$ give $f(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly in $\overline H$ at infinity. For completeness the boundary contour step is valid for any scalar $f$ holomorphic on $H:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on $\overline H$, with $C^1$ real boundary restriction and $f(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on $\overline H$ at infinity. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$. Use the real intervals from $\omega-R$ to $\omega-\eta$ and $\omega+\eta$ to $\omega+R$, a clockwise upper semicircle of radius $\eta$ about $\omega$, and the counterclockwise large upper semicircle of radius $R$ about $\omega$. For $\delta>0$ apply [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]] to $f(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ on $D_\delta:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$. This open domain is star-shaped about any point $\omega+iA$, $A>0$, so the contour is null-homotopic there and the integrand is holomorphic. All contour pieces lie in $D_\delta$; no analytic extension of $f$ across the real boundary is assumed. On each fixed contour, continuity on a compact closed-half-plane neighborhood gives $f(z+i\delta)\to f(z)$ uniformly as $\delta\downarrow0$ by [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], and [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]] transfers the zero contour identity to $f(z)/(z-\omega)$. The large arc has $|z-\omega|=R$, $|z|\ge R-|\omega|$ and length $\pi R$, hence its contribution is $O(1/R)$. Parametrizing the clockwise small arc by $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$ gives $-i\pi f(\omega)+o(1)$. Locally the divided difference $[f(\xi)-f(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded because the boundary is $C^1$; the constant term cancels under the symmetric indentation. The tails are absolutely integrable by $f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)=O(|\xi|^{-2})$. First $\eta\downarrow0$, then $R\to\infty$ therefore gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi f(\omega)$ and the two real/imaginary formulas. Apply that boundary-contour argument to $f$, multiply both formulas by the real factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^n$, and add the complex polynomial $P$. At $\omega_0$ the factor vanishes and the removable Taylor identity gives the asserted Taylor value. The imaginary numerator subtracts the full complex $P$; it cannot be omitted.
For the distinct constitutive branch, multiplication by $(-i\omega)^j$ is the derivative multiplier on the stipulated monochromatic histories, so the transfer polynomial is exactly $Q$. Derivatives at a time are determined by a history agreeing on its whole past, including its endpoint, and the convolution is causal; hence their finite sum is causal on histories with the stated bounded continuous derivatives. The residual $\chi-Q=\chi_K$ satisfies [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]] entrywise. Without that lemma's AC and integrability conditions a merely integrable causal kernel still gives a bounded upper-half-plane holomorphic response, but does not automatically supply these principal values or Taylor continuation. The stated additional analytic assumptions, not causality alone, govern the Taylor branch.

proposed_subjects.title: Causal convolution response, transfer function and dispersion relations
proposed_subjects.reference: completed-expansion-arguments.md#D1-D2 (compact and W^{1,1} integrable causal branches), assembled with the passivity quadratic form
proposed_subjects.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the smooth Riemann/Lebesgue comparison route below; in clause (c), also assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) inherited from the AC supplier. Let $d\ge1$. All kernels below are real $d\times d$ matrix kernels and all histories are $\mathbb R^d$-valued; conditions on matrices are read entrywise, and $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ means entrywise Lebesgue integrability on $(0,\infty)$.

(a) (Causal convolution.) Let $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and continuous. Then for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the integral $P(t):=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely, $$|P_j(t)|\le\sum_{k=1}^d\Bigl(\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}|E_k(s)|\Bigr)\int_0^\infty|K_{jk}(s)|\,ds\qquad(j=1,\dots,d),$$ the response $P$ is bounded and continuous, the map $E\mapsto P$ is linear, and it is causal: if $E_1,E_2$ are bounded continuous and coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$, then their responses coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

(b) (Compact branch.) If $K\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (smooth, with compact support contained in the open half-line), then the transfer function $$\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for every real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$. For any $b>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$, the full entire-plane bound is $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}\|K_{jk}\prime\prime\|_1|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$. Its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi$$ for every real $\omega$.

(c) (Integrable branch.) If instead $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is locally absolutely continuous entrywise in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]] on every compact subinterval of $[0,\infty)$, with $K\prime$ its almost-everywhere derivative with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $s\mapsto sK(s)$ in $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$, then $\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is well defined and holomorphic on the open upper half-plane $\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on the closed upper half-plane with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, satisfies the same pair of dispersion relations for every real $\omega$, and is bounded on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ by $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K_{jk}'\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}$ for $|z|\ge1$; for an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ define $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}:=\chi_\infty+\chi$ and apply the relations to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$.

(d) (Monochromatic work and passivity.) Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^d$, and let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be a real parameter (a response normalization; the equivalence below is independent of its value). Put $E(t):=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{-i\omega t})$ and $P(t):=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, real parts taken componentwise and $\chi(\omega)$ acting by matrix multiplication. Then, with $T:=2\pi/\omega$ and the Euclidean dot product on $\mathbb R^d$, $$\frac1T\int_0^T E(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),\qquad e^*\chi(\omega)e:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\overline{e_j}\,\chi_{jk}(\omega)\,e_k,$$ and this period-averaged work is nonnegative for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$ if and only if the Hermitian part $M(\omega):=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$ satisfies $e^*M(\omega)e\ge0$ for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$.
proposed_subjects.strategy:
Proof technique: direct, branch by branch; clausal tags below indicate the cited tools.

(a) For each $j$ and $t$, absolute convergence and the displayed bound follow from $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$, the triangle inequality for integrals and monotonicity of the nonnegative integral over the measurable set $(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]). Linearity in $E$ is linearity of the integral. Continuity in $t$: if $t_n\to t$ then $K_{jk}(s)E_k(t_n-s)\to K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)$ for every $s$ with the integrable dominating function $(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}|$, so dominated convergence gives $P(t_n)\to P(t)$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Causality: for $t\le t_0$ and every $s\ge0$ the argument $t-s$ lies in $(-\infty,t_0]$, so replacing $E$ by a history agreeing with it there changes no integrand value and hence no integral.

(b) Holomorphy is obtained from the real-parameter differentiation theorem rather than by differentiating in the complex variable directly. Writing $z=x+iy$, the integrand $K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}=K_{jk}(s)e^{ixs}e^{-ys}$ has continuous partials in $x$ and $y$; because $K_{jk}$ has compact support, on every compact set of parameters $(x,y)$ the partials are dominated by a fixed multiple of $|K_{jk}|(1+|s|)$, an integrable function, so [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied in the two real parameters gives the continuous partials $\partial_x\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty isK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ and $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty(-s)K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). These satisfy $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=-\int sK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\int isK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\,\partial_x\chi_{jk}$, the Cauchy--Riemann equations for the pair $(\partial_x\chi_{jk},\partial_y\chi_{jk})$ with the identification $f=u+iv$; since the partials exist on a neighbourhood and are continuous, [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]] makes $\chi_{jk}$ holomorphic, and because the same argument is available at every $z\in\mathbb C$, each entry is entire ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). Iterating gives $\chi_{jk}^{(k)}(z)=\int_0^\infty(is)^kK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$. For the reality identity at real $\omega$: conjugation is an isometry and a real-field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) and the series defining the complex exponential converges everywhere ([[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]); conjugating the partial sums termwise and passing to the limit along the isometry gives $\overline{e^{i\omega s}}=e^{-i\omega s}$, so conjugating the defining integral of $\chi_{jk}$ and using that $K_{jk}$ is real gives $\overline{\chi_{jk}(\omega)}=\int_0^\infty K_{jk}(s)e^{-i\omega s}\,ds=\chi_{jk}(-\omega)$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). On $[0,b]$, apply [[thm-integration-by-parts]] twice to the real and imaginary parts of the smooth exponential and real smooth kernel (first $K$, then $K\prime$). All derivatives are continuous and Riemann integrable; [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]] transfers each compact-interval identity to the Lebesgue integrals. With vanishing endpoint values because $K$ vanishes near $0$ and beyond $b$, these identities give $\chi_{jk}(z)=-z^{-2}\int_0^\infty K_{jk}''(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ for $z\ne0$, hence the stated upper-half-plane $|z|^{-2}$ bound; for arbitrary complex $z$, $|e^{izs}|\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ on the support gives the full entire-plane bound. For the dispersion relations fix real $\omega$ and form a contour consisting of the interval $[-R,R]$ indented above $\omega$ on a clockwise semicircle of radius $\delta$, closed by the large semicircle of radius $R$ in the upper half-plane; on the indented domain the integrand $\chi_{jk}(z)/(z-\omega)$ is holomorphic, so Cauchy's theorem for null-homotopic loops gives vanishing total integral ([[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]]). The large arc contributes at most $\pi R\sup_{|z|=R,\operatorname{Im}z\ge0}|\chi_{jk}|/(R-|\omega|)\to0$ by the $|z|^{-2}$ bound. The small arc contributes $-i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)+o(1)$ as $\delta\to0$, by continuity of $\chi_{jk}$ on the closed upper half-plane, which follows from dominated convergence as in (a) ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). The remaining real integral converges to its principal value: near $\omega$ subtract the constant $\chi_{jk}(\omega)$ so that the divided difference $[\chi_{jk}(\xi)-\chi_{jk}(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded, and at infinity use the $|z|^{-2}$ decay. Letting $\delta\to0$, $R\to\infty$ gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\chi_{jk}(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)$; separating real and imaginary parts yields the displayed pair because $i(a+ib)=-b+ia$.

(c) This is precisely the content of the cited integrable-causal-dispersion lemma: that item proves, under exactly these hypotheses, the holomorphy on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]), the closed-half-plane bound, the boundary regularity and the two principal-value formulas, and records the instantaneous-response subtraction ([[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]). The present theorem assembles the response, its transfer function and the passivity relation around that lemma; its explicit AC definition and Lebesgue FTC/integration-by-parts route apply entrywise under the inherited Countable Choice and Dependent Choice; its boundary contour uses vertical shifts before passing to the real boundary.

(d) The period-average of a product of real parts of complex exponentials is supplied by [[lem-em-period-average]], which states exactly $\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})dt=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(a\cdot\overline d)$; applying it with $a=e$ and $d=(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e$ (the derivative of $t\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, computed with the chain rule) gives $$\frac1T\int_0^TE(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(e\cdot\overline{(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e}\Bigr)=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),$$ using $e\cdot\overline{\chi(\omega)e}=\overline{e^*\chi(\omega)e}$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-iz)=\operatorname{Im}z$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]). Finally $e^*M(\omega)e=(e^*\chi(\omega)e-e^*\chi(\omega)^*e)/(2i)=\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi(\omega)e)$ because $M(\omega)$ is the Hermitian part of $\chi(\omega)$, so nonnegativity of the displayed average for every $e$ is exactly the stated quadratic-form condition. The logical independence of causality and this positivity (the design's 'no sign of dissipation follows merely from causality') is exhibited on the companion example page by a kernel satisfying (c) whose quadratic form is strictly negative.

proposed_subjects.title: Hypothesis boundaries: a causal response without passivity, and the fixed-retarded-time flux limit
proposed_subjects.reference: mathematical-example-verifications.md#ex-em-causal-response-and-radiation-prerequisites-hypothesis-boundaries; clause (ii) added by this scaffolder to exercise the second theorem's declared dependency (recorded in the batch notes)
proposed_subjects.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the surface-integral conventions used by [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]].

(i) (Causality without passivity.) In this clause also assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]), inherited from the exact AC supplier. Let $K(s):=-e^{-s}$ for $s\ge0$. Then $K$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ (indeed $K'=e^{-s}=-K$, $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=1$ and $\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$), so the integrable branch of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] applies: $P(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)ds$ is a bounded causal linear response on bounded continuous histories, its transfer function is $\chi(z)=-1/(1-iz)$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, and its boundary value $\chi(\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ for every $\omega>0$. Hence the Hermitian part $M(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)$ is strictly negative, not positive semidefinite, and the monochromatic period-averaged work of clause (d) of that theorem is strictly negative for $d=1$, every $e\ne0$ and every $\omega>0$ (with any response normalization $\varepsilon_0>0$), although the response is causal and its entry satisfies the dispersion relations of clause (c). Nonnegative period-averaged work (passivity) is therefore an additional condition on the model, not a consequence of temporal causality.

(ii) (The flux limit needs fixed retarded time.) In the setting of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]], fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and $n\in S^2$, and let $r>\max\{2a,\;a+c(t-t_0)\}$. Then for every $y\in B_a$ one has $R=|rn-y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$, so $t-R/c<t_0$; by hypothesis (H1) of that theorem the functions $\rho,\rho_t,\mathbf J,\mathbf J_t$ all vanish at $(y,t-R/c)$, so every integrand in the field formulas of clause (a) of that theorem vanishes and $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$, hence $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$. Therefore $\int_{S^2}r^2\,n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)\,d\Omega(n)=0$ for all such $r$: at fixed observation time the far-zone flux integral is identically zero beyond the light cone of the compact spacetime support, whereas clause (c) of that theorem is a limit at fixed retarded time. The retarded-time formulation cannot be replaced by a fixed-observation-time one.

Proof technique: direct computation and direct substitution into the two cited theorems.

(i) The real exponential is differentiable with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]) and $\exp(-s)>0$ with $\exp(-s)=1/\exp(s)$ ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]), so $s\mapsto K(s)=-e^{-s}$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K'=e^{-s}=-K$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). For every $N>0$ the Newton-Leibniz formula gives $\int_0^Ne^{-s}ds=1-e^{-N}$ and integration by parts (with $u=s$, $v=-e^{-s}$) gives $\int_0^Nse^{-s}ds=1-(1+N)e^{-N}$ ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], [[thm-integration-by-parts]]); the continuous real integrands have the same Lebesgue integrals by [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]]; [[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]] proves the explicit $C^1$ kernel is absolutely continuous on each compact interval in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]; the displayed Newton-Leibniz integral representations agree with the Lebesgue FTC under this regularity. Thus it has the absolute-continuity property required by the integrable branch of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]], and passing to the limit with monotone convergence for the nonnegative integrands gives $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$, so $K,K',sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). Clause (a) of the theorem therefore gives the bounded causal response. For the transfer function, fix real $\omega$; the complex exponential is entire with derivative itself and the complex chain rule gives that $s\mapsto F(s)=\exp((-1+i\omega)s)/(-1+i\omega)$ is a primitive of $s\mapsto\exp((-1+i\omega)s)$ on $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]], [[def-complex-exponential]]), so the fundamental theorem for complex line integrals along the interval path $[0,N]\ni s\mapsto s$ gives $\int_{[0,N]}\exp((-1+i\omega)s)\,ds=F(N)-F(0)$ ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-for-complex-line-integrals]], [[def-complex-primitive]], [[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]], [[thm-riemann-stieltjes-and-parametric-contour-integrals-agree]]). Hence $\int_0^N(-e^{-s})e^{i\omega s}ds=-(F(N)-F(0))$, and $\left|e^{(-1+i\omega)N}\right|=e^{-N}\to0$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]); letting $N\to\infty$ with dominated convergence for the integrands dominated by $e^{-s}$ gives $\chi(\omega)=-1/(1-i\omega)$, and the same computation with $z$ in place of $\omega$ gives $\chi(z)=-1/(1-iz)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Taking real and imaginary parts ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) gives $\chi(\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ and $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ because $\omega>0$. With $d=1$, $e=1$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$, clause (d) of the theorem gives period-averaged work $\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)<0$ and $M(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)<0$, so the passivity condition fails while causality holds: this witnesses the logical independence recorded in the theorem's proof discussion.

(ii) For $y\in B_a$ the reverse triangle inequality gives $R=|rn-y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), hence $t-R/c<t_0$ and all four source functions vanish at the arguments appearing in the field integrals of clause (a) of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]]; each integrand is identically zero on $B_a$, so $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$ and therefore $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=\mu_0^{-1}n\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$. The surface integral of the zero function vanishes ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), so the fixed-observation-time flux integral is $0$ for every $r>\max\{2a,a+c(t-t_0)\}$, while the limit displayed in clause (c) of that theorem is taken with $u$ fixed and $r\to\infty$ along $t=u+r/c$; the two formulations therefore differ and the retarded-time one is essential.

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

supplier_registry.exact_interface:
Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. The reverse derivation is standard and is not needed anywhere in
this library, so it is not carried out; every use below prescribes $x_0$.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$. The function $f$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** if the limit

$$ \lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\ne0,\ a+h\in U}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$

exists in the metric of [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. Its value is the **complex derivative** of $f$ at $a$, denoted $f'(a)$. The increments are nonzero and remain in the domain; because $U$ is open, all sufficiently small increments are allowed.

The function $f$ is **holomorphic on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. The word analytic is reserved for the local power-series notion.

supplier_registry.exact_interface:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. supplier_registry.exact_interface:
Let $d\ge1$. All kernels below are real $d\times d$ matrix kernels and all histories are $\mathbb R^d$-valued; conditions on matrices are read entrywise, and $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ means entrywise Lebesgue integrability on $(0,\infty)$.

(a) (Causal convolution.) Let $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and continuous. Then for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the integral $P(t):=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely, $$|P_j(t)|\le\sum_{k=1}^d\Bigl(\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}|E_k(s)|\Bigr)\int_0^\infty|K_{jk}(s)|\,ds\qquad(j=1,\dots,d),$$ the response $P$ is bounded and continuous, the map $E\mapsto P$ is linear, and it is causal: if $E_1,E_2$ are bounded continuous and coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$, then their responses coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

(b) (Compact branch.) If $K\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (smooth, with compact support contained in the open half-line), then the transfer function $$\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for every real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$, and its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi$$ for every real $\omega$.

(c) (Integrable branch.) If instead $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is locally absolutely continuous (absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $[0,\infty)$) with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $s\mapsto sK(s)$ in $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$, then $\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is well defined and holomorphic on the open upper half-plane $\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on the closed upper half-plane with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, satisfies the same pair of dispersion relations for every real $\omega$, and is bounded on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ by $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K_{jk}'\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}$ for $|z|\ge1$; for an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ the relations hold with $\chi$ replaced by $\chi-\chi_\infty$.

(d) (Monochromatic work and passivity.) Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^d$, and let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be a real parameter (a response normalization; the equivalence below is independent of its value). Put $E(t):=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{-i\omega t})$ and $P(t):=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, real parts taken componentwise and $\chi(\omega)$ acting by matrix multiplication. Then, with $T:=2\pi/\omega$ and the Euclidean dot product on $\mathbb R^d$, $$\frac1T\int_0^T E(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),\qquad e^*\chi(\omega)e:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\overline{e_j}\,\chi_{jk}(\omega)\,e_k,$$ and this period-averaged work is nonnegative for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$ if and only if the Hermitian part $M(\omega):=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$ satisfies $e^*M(\omega)e\ge0$ for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$.

Let $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $a>0$ and $t_0<T$ be constants, let $\rho\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ and $\mathbf J\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfy (H1) $\rho(y,v)=\mathbf J(y,v)=0$ whenever $|y|>a$ or $v\notin[t_0,T]$, and (H2) $\partial_v\rho+\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. For $x$ with $r:=|x|\ge2a$ define the retarded scalar and vector potentials $$\varphi(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0c^2}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad \mathbf A(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\mathbf J(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy,$$ and the fields $\mathbf E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$, $\mathbf B:=\nabla\times\mathbf A$, where the derivatives are taken in $x$ and all objects are read on $\{|x|\ge2a\}$.

(a) (Fields as retarded integrals.) On the open set $\{|x|>2a\}$ the potentials $\varphi,\mathbf A$ are of class $C^\infty$ in $(x,t)$, and there $$\mathbf E(x,t)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Bigl[\frac{\mathbf N}{R^2}c^2\rho\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)+\frac{\mathbf N}{cR}c\,\rho_t\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)-\frac{\mathbf J_t\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)}{R}\Bigr]dy,$$$$\mathbf B(x,t)=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathbf N\times\Bigl[\frac{\mathbf J(y,t-\frac Rc)}{R^2}+\frac{\mathbf J_t(y,t-\frac Rc)}{cR}\Bigr]dy,$$ where $R:=|x-y|$, $\mathbf N:=(x-y)/R$, and $\rho_t,\mathbf J_t$ are the partial derivatives in the second variable. Moreover, on $\{|x|\ge2a\}\times[t_0,T]$, $\varphi$ and each component of $\mathbf A$ coincide with the corresponding solution constructed in the wave Cauchy problem of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] for zero Cauchy data at $t_0$ and scalar source $h=\mu_0c^2\rho$, respectively $h=\mu_0 J_k$.

(b) (Uniform far-zone expansion.) For $n\in S^2$ and $u\in[t_0,T]$ put $\mathbf I(n,u):=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$ and $\mathbf V(n,u):=\partial_u\mathbf I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$. Then $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy=\frac1c\,n\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$, and there are constants $\Gamma_E,\Gamma_B$, depending only on $a,c,\mu_0$ and on the suprema of $|\rho|,|\rho_t|,|\rho_{tt}|,|\mathbf J|,|\mathbf J_t|,|\mathbf J_{tt}|$ on $\overline B_a\times[t_0,T]$, such that for every $n\in S^2$, $u\in[t_0,T]$ and $r\ge2a$, with $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times\mathbf V(n,u))$, $$\Bigl|\mathbf E(rn,u+\tfrac rc)-\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2},\qquad \Bigl|\mathbf B(rn,u+\tfrac rc)-\frac{n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)}{c}\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_B}{r^2}.$$

(c) (Retarded-time flux limit.) Let $\mathbf S:=\mu_0^{-1}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ and let $d\Omega$ be the surface measure on $S^2$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]). Then for every $u\in[t_0,T]$, $$\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2\,n\cdot\mathbf S\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)\,d\Omega(n)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}\bigl|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)\bigr|^2\,d\Omega(n).$$ This is a limit at fixed retarded time $u$, not at fixed observation time $t$; no decay or boundary condition at spatial infinity is assumed beyond the compact spatial support in (H1).

Let $F$ be a primitive of a continuous function $f$ on an open set containing the trace of a rectifiable contour $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$. If $F'=f$ is continuous, then
$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=F(\gamma(b))-F(\gamma(a)).$$

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.
